The ending -ción is always stressed: ha-bi-ta-CIÓN, es-ta-CIÓN. In Spain it is read “thyon”.
Z is read like “th” (Spain) or “s” (Latin America): azul = “a-thool”, izquierda = “ith-kyer-da”.
HAY is a wonderfully simple word: it has ONE form, for both singular and plural. It means “there is” or “there are” when you say WHAT is somewhere.
It is read “eye” (the h is silent). To remember it: “Hay” sounds like “I” — and “I” see something there.
2. HAY or ESTÁ? The clear rule
Both are often translated as “is”, but they are not interchangeable. It all depends on the word that follows:
→ you say where something KNOWN is
In the flat there is a bathroom. (I learn that it exists)
The bathroom is on the right. (I know about it, I ask where it is)
Wrong: “Hay el baño a la derecha”. After “hay” you never put el / la / mi.
Unlike English, the adjective usually goes AFTER the noun and agrees with it: un sofá azul (a blue sofa), una casa blanca (a white house).
For a permanent description (big, old, blue) you use SER: “La casa es grande”. For a temporary state, ESTAR: “La casa está limpia” (the house is clean right now).
4. Where is it? Prepositions of place
“de + el” must become “del”: al lado DEL sofá (next to the sofa). “de + la” stays “de la”: al lado de la mesa.
5. “Es de mi abuela” — whose it is
For “it’s someone’s” you use SER + de: “La mesa es de mi abuela” = The table is my grandmother’s.
Spanish has no “’s”. Everything English says with “X’s” is done with “de”: la casa de Ana = Ana’s house.
“La cocina” is known: where it is → ESTÁ.
